claims.text: A model incorporating atomic mass variance, force-constant dispersion, and lattice-distortion descriptors will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than composition-only approaches.
Chemical disorder in HEAs produces atomic-mass and force-constant fluctuations.
Atomic-mass variance, force-constant dispersion, and lattice distortion directly correlate with enhanced phonon scattering.
The target materials are single-phase, disordered, equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA solid solutions without secondary intermetallic phases.
The predictive approach uses atomic-mass variance, bond-stiffness variation, and predicted lattice distortion to screen HEA candidates.
An inert environment from room temperature to 500°C will minimize extrinsic scattering effects during thermal measurements.
Multi-element mixing in HEAs produces enhanced lattice distortion.
Multi-element mixing in HEAs produces force-constant disorder.
Lattice distortion and force-constant disorder increase phonon-scattering rates.
Atomic-scale mass and bond-strength fluctuations reduce phonon lifetimes.
Atomic-scale mass and bond-strength fluctuations reduce phonon mean free paths.
Reduced phonon lifetimes and mean free paths lower lattice thermal conductivity.
HEAs selected by the descriptor-based model will exhibit significantly lower lattice thermal conductivity than candidates selected by composition-only models.
The improvement over composition-only predictions will be notable, although its absolute percentage is uncertain.
The approach primarily applies to single-phase HEA solid solutions in which configurational disorder dominates phonon transport.
The approach may not apply to multiphase or intermetallic systems because phase boundaries and other scattering mechanisms can dominate thermal transport.
Model accuracy depends on the quality and representativeness of the descriptor training set.
Inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering can be used to investigate HEA phonon dynamics and lifetimes.
